items.title: From teachers to academics professional transformation and social mobility in Indonesia
items.abstract: The transformation of teachers into scientist-lecturers has emerged as a strategic issue in response to rapid advances in science, technology, and globalization, requiring shifts in professional identity, competence, and social positioning. This study employed a mixed-methods approach using a sequential explanatory design. The study collected quantitative data from one hundred and five (105) respondents. The study analyzed these data using regression analysis and structural equation modeling (SEM). This was followed by a qualitative inquiry involving interviews with six (6) participants and three (3) significant others, whose data were analyzed using the Gioia method. Quantitative findings indicate that professional transformation is significantly associated with social mobility; however, the direct effect becomes non-significant after incorporating the transition into scientist-lecturers into the model, providing empirical support for a primary indirect effect and a potential mediating role of the scientist-lecturer transition. Qualitative results reveal that this transformation is shaped by the interaction of intrinsic motivation, learning orientation, institutional support, and policy context, alongside dynamic processes of cognitive, social, and identity adaptation. The findings suggest that professional transformation is multidimensional and non-linear, involving interacting processes of cognitive, social, and professional identity adaptation.

items.title: From the fluency fallacy to the micro-to-macro validity gap: opportunities and pitfalls of LLMs in social simulation
items.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into social simulation has generated considerable enthusiasm, but also raises substantial methodological and epistemological challenges. This critical review examines the use of LLMs as cognitive or decision-making components of simulated agents from a computational social science perspective. Rather than treating the psychological evaluation of LLMs as separate from simulation mechanics, we argue that their behavioral and epistemic limitations can become systemic vulnerabilities when scaled to multi-agent societies. We first map the rapidly evolving landscape of LLM-driven platforms, ranging from small narrative sandboxes to population-scale and spatially structured simulations. We then develop a unified critical framework for analyzing the Micro-to-Macro Validity Gap: the propagation, nonlinear amplification, or convergent contraction of micro-level limitations—including hallucinations, stochastic inconsistency, representational biases, and alignment effects—into agent-level distortions (such as average persona convergence) and macro-level risks (such as artificial consensus and behavioral homogenization), while exposing evaluators to epistemic vulnerabilities such as the Fluency Fallacy and automation bias. We identify contexts in which LLM-based agents offer genuine operational value, including serious games, participatory environments, and exploratory modeling, while distinguishing these uses from confirmatory research with unconstrained models and precise social forecasting. Finally, we examine theory-driven hybrid architectures that embed LLMs within explicit, mechanistic, and reproducible Agent-Based modeling (ABM) frameworks. We argue that such architectures offer a promising but not sufficient path toward improving epistemic control: their validity depends on multi-level evaluation of environmental dynamics, individual behavior, cross-level interactions, and aggregate outcomes, and they remain vulnerable to the risk of physics washing.

items.title: From tools to sense-making: Designing a human-centred AI workshop
items.abstract: Generative AI raises identity- and values-level questions for higher education staff. Yet professional development in this space remains largely focused on individualised technical and pedagogical skill and capability development, rather than providing structured opportunities for the collective sense-making such questions require. This paper describes the design and delivery of a human-centred workshop developed for a team of higher education third space practitioners to support collective sense-making and values negotiation around AI use. Drawing on reflective practitioner inquiry, we describe the design principles that shaped the workshop and the practical constraints within which it was delivered. We reflect on what worked, including the value of structured formats in supporting deeper engagement, and of workshop artefacts as an evolving record of shared thinking. We suggest this design offers a transferable approach for other educator teams grappling with similar uncertainty, and propose that professional development for AI should complement skills-focused approaches with structured space for the collective exploration of values, judgement, and human agency.

items.title: From tools to teammates: When children and AI create together in early childhood education
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into learning environments, its role is shifting from a passive tool to an active partner in meaning-making and creative expression. This study explores how young children engage in co-creative learning with AI through adults and examines the implications of these interactions for reimagining human–AI partnerships in early childhood education. Sixteen children (aged 5-6) from a single preschool classroom first drew an original character and then worked individually alongside a researcher to generate an AI-based version of that character using Gemini, with up to three iterative prompts per child. Data from classroom observations, interaction records, and reflective discussions were analysed using thematic analysis to understand children’s interaction dynamics. Initial findings reveal one key dimension of co-creative engagement. Children appreciated AI’s ability to extend and transform their visual ideas, yet emphasised the importance of maintaining personal authorship and manual control, highlighting an emerging sense of creative agency in human–AI collaboration. Building on these findings, the study proposes a vision of AI as a creative teammate that amplifies children's imagination while preserving human intentionality and ownership.

items.title: GameRealm: Grounding Visual Learning in Interactive Games
items.abstract: Visual foundation models are central to physical intelligence, yet their development remains constrained by fragmented training datasets, inconsistent annotation quality, and limited multimodal supervision. To address these challenges, we introduce GameRealm, a large-scale, richly annotated dataset that grounds visual observations in synchronized, game-native supervision. GameRealm encompasses over 120 million RGB frames and 1,000 hours of gameplay footage across all views. Beyond its unprecedented scale, GameRealm provides rich multimodal supervision, including metric depth, camera parameters, synchronized audio, control inputs, and 3D point trajectories. Its diversity further extends to flexible view configurations, spanning single-view, stereo, multi-view, and panoramic recordings. To enable scalable acquisition across diverse game environments, we develop a unified data collection pipeline that combines human-operated interaction with agentic exploration. Extensive experiments across diverse visual learning tasks demonstrate that GameRealm consistently strengthens visual foundation models in both visual generation and geometric learning. These results establish GameRealm as a versatile and valuable data resource, unlocking new opportunities for advancing visual intelligence.

items.title: GapLeak: When Privacy-Preserving LLM-based Web Agents Become a Privacy Risk
items.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based web agents rely on data minimization and least privilege to protect user privacy. We show that these principles are necessary but insufficient: they constrain authorized sources, but not higher-sensitivity sources that remain reachable. A website can request a field unavailable from authorized sources, creating an information gap. To complete the task, a goal-driven agent may escalate to reachable but unauthorized sources and disclose accumulated sensitive information. We formalize this vulnerability as GapLeak, where an adversary exploits a legitimate web form without prompt injection or other malicious instructions. We evaluate GapLeak on three web-agent frameworks and six LLMs from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI across recruitment, e-commerce, travel, and healthcare. GapLeak induces an average unauthorized disclosure of approximately 37%. The information gap is the primary driver: eliminating it reduces disclosure by more than 50%. Existing instruction-level defenses based on least privilege partially mitigate the vulnerability but often reduce task success. We propose submission-time verification, which filters unauthorized content before form submission, eliminating over 96% of unauthorized disclosures while preserving task success.

items.title: GenAI and novice programmers’ conceptual understanding: A systematic review
items.abstract: Programming education remains challenging for novice learners, and the emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has introduced new opportunities and challenges for learning programming. While existing research reports a range of potential benefits, the influence of GenAI on conceptual understanding remains underexplored. This systematic literature review investigates the role of GenAI in influencing novice programmers’ conceptual understanding in higher education programming contexts. Guided by the PRISMA framework, empirical studies published between 2022 and 2026 were reviewed and synthesised using a conceptual understanding framework comprising three dimensions: understanding programming constructs, reasoning about program behaviour, and developing mental models of program execution. The findings indicate that GenAI primarily functions as a learning support tool that may enhance understanding of programming constructs. However, evidence is less conclusive regarding reasoning about program behaviour and is extremely limited in relation to mental models of program execution. The review suggests that the effects of GenAI are concentrated in more surface-level dimensions of understanding and do not consistently translate into deeper conceptual understanding. The study identifies important gaps in current research and outlines directions for further investigation.

items.title: GenAI avatars to promote negotiation and AI skills among student presentations
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has radically disrupted higher education assessment paradigms (Chung, 2024). Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. This research addresses a critical gap in current Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) literature by investigating the following central question: How are students’ AI literacy and negotiation skills developed when conversing with GenAI avatars as part of a viva presentation? Adopting a design-based research methodology, this project emphasizes the iterative refinement of an educational intervention within an authentic setting (Hoadley & Campos, 2022; Scott et al., 2020). The study is currently in its first implementation cycle within a major tertiary institution, featuring a sample size of 150 second-year Project Management students. Participants are required to defend a project proposal during a live, assessable viva presentation conducted with a customized VirtualSpeech avatar trained to act as a client. This oral format diminishes the appeal of cognitive offloading because students must defend their reasoning under unseen, real-time questioning (Sotiriadou et al., 2020; Tan, 2026). Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. This research significantly advances TEL research and practice by providing a protocol for proactive AI integration. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

items.title: General intellect y gestión algorítmica. La regulación del trabajo en plataformas digitales
items.abstract: This article analyses transformations of work under cognitive and platform capitalism, placing algorithmic management at the centre as a contemporary form of labour control. Through a critical dialogue with technological determinism, it draws on Castells and Vercellone to explain how knowledge and workers’ cognitive capacities have become central sources of capital valorisation. Within this framework, algorithms operate not as neutral technical tools but as sociotechnical devices that organise, supervise and discipline labour in a continuous, opaque and delocalised manner. The article shows how platform companies condense long-term historical tendencies by articulating concentrated digital infrastructure, large-scale data capture and narratives of individual autonomy. Analysis of the mechanisms of algorithmic direction, evaluation and discipline demonstrates that control over the labour process shifts towards the appropriation of collective knowledge, that is, of the general intellect. Finally, the article examines the regulatory frameworks of Spain and the European Union, the four Latin American cases currently in force, and ILO Convention No. 193, adopted in 2026. It argues that algorithmic transparency is a necessary but insufficient condition: it becomes transformative only when accompanied by the collective capacity to contest the design of these systems, and not merely to know their effects.

items.title: Generative AI and Cognitive Autonomy in Cameroonian Higher Education: A Conditional Amplification Framework for Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly entering higher education, yet its implications for learner autonomy remain unsettled, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined how pedagogical GAI use relates to self-regulated learning, cognitive engagement, augmented cognitive autonomy (ACA), and deep learning in six Cameroonian higher education institutions. Quantitative data from 812 students and faculty members were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, followed by 24 semi-structured interviews. GAI use was positively associated with self-regulation, while self-regulation and cognitive engagement sequentially mediated its relationship with ACA. ACA was strongly associated with deep learning. AI literacy and institutional governance strengthened the relationship between GAI use and ACA. Qualitative findings revealed both reflective, dialogic uses and cognitive delegation. The findings support an emerging Augmented Cognitive Autonomy framework in which GAI amplifies learning conditionally, depending on users' regulatory capacities and institutional support, with implications for equity and human capability development.

items.title: GST Compliance Reconciliation and Vouching Verification in a Small Chartered Accountancy Practice: An Applied Case Study from India
items.abstract: Goods and Services Tax (GST) compliance and vouching are usually taught as separate subjects, one belonging to indirect taxation and the other to auditing. In small Chartered Accountancy (CA) practices in India, however, the same junior staff perform both, on the same client files and within the same monthly cycle. This paper examines how the two work-streams complement each other as an integrated, reconciliation-first assurance process. Using a single-case, participant-observation design, it draws on an eight-week on-the-job training placement (22 June to 22 August 2026) at a mid-sized CA practice in Maharashtra, India. Process observations, a structured learning diary and template-based working papers were used to document the monthly GST compliance cycle and a transaction-level vouching routine. Because client information is confidential, the analysis uses an anonymised, illustrative entity whose figures were constructed to reflect patterns observed in practice. In the illustration, outward supplies matched fully across the sales register, GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B, while an Input Tax Credit (ITC) mismatch of ₹7,200 in April, caused by a supplier's late filing, fell to ₹4,500 in May and cleared by June. An eleven-voucher vouching sample produced two exceptions, both procedural. The paper argues that vouching and GST reconciliation test the same books against two different evidence sources, so that errors escaping one check tend to be caught by the other. It closes with recommendations on standard checklists, named ownership of reconciliation and a shared mismatch tracker, and discusses limitations arising from the single-firm, short-duration and illustrative-data design. Keywords: Goods and Services Tax; Input Tax Credit; GSTR-2B reconciliation; vouching; audit evidence; chartered accountancy practice; workplace learning

items.title: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation
items.abstract: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

items.title: HarmoHOI: Harmonizing Appearance and 3D Motion for Multi-view Hand-Object Interaction Synthesis
items.abstract: Hand-Object Interaction (HOI) synthesis is a cornerstone for animation production and embodied AI. Despite the strong priors of video foundation models, multi-view consistent HOI synthesis remains challenging due to complex hand motions and occlusions. We present HarmoHOI, a unified diffusion framework that jointly and harmoniously generates synchronized multi-view HOI videos and globally aligned 3D point tracks. Our core insight is that robust multi-view consistency fundamentally requires globally aligned 3D geometry and motion. To this end, we propose a Mixture of Multi-view Diffusion Transformer that co-models RGB videos and 3D point tracks. By representing point tracks as pseudo-videos, we align 3D geometric signals with the 2D latent space of foundation models, thereby minimizing the domain gap and easing adaptation of priors. To further ensure geometry consistency, we introduce Global Motion Aligning Diffusion, which refines coarse point tracks into metric-scale, globally aligned 3D trajectories. HarmoHOI enables on-the-fly co-evolution of 2D appearance and 3D motion during denoising. To overcome the scarcity of multi-view HOI data, we employ a hybrid data curriculum learning strategy that successfully transfers generic priors from single-view data to synchronized multi-view generation. Experimental results show that HarmoHOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in visual quality, motion plausibility, and multi-view geometric consistency. Code for this paper are at https://droliven.github.io/HarmoHOI_project/.

items.title: HiGAI-Net: Hierarchical Encrypted Traffic Classification for Generative AI Services
items.abstract: The Radio Access Network (RAN) today does not have a reliable way to identify GenAI traffic (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, or Google Gemini traffic) at the bearer level. TLS~1.3 moves SNI into the encrypted handshake record, and Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) removes it entirely from passive inspection; Gemini has partly shifted to QUIC where SNI visibility also depends on whether ECH is deployed. Without per-flow application identity, differentiated QoS for GenAI services is not possible. HiGAI-Net tackles this using only packet-header metadata, stacking three independently trained classifiers: a binary AI/Non-AI gate (98.5 % weighted F1), a per-service resolver across ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini (86.4 %), and a text-vs-voice/video mode classifier (61.0 %). The core innovation is a suite of sliding-window temporal features that track how DL/UL byte-ratios evolve within a session -- the per-quarter and per-half ratio trends, a trend differential $ΔR$, and a streaming regularity index. Tested on 44,492 labeled flows, gradient-boosted tree models consistently outperformed all deep-learning variants; a per-flow label cache brings amortised inference below 1~$μ$s per packet.

items.title: Highly Superficial Flexible Coil Array for 1.5T MRI: Diagnostic Quality Evaluation Compared to Conventional Technology
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To assess the imaging performance, thermal behavior, and patient acceptance of a novel 3-channel flexible coil array for 1.5T MRI (64 MHz), compared to a conventional 16-channel flexible coil. METHODS: A lightweight array with three 60 mm copper loops and a compact 32×15 mm electronics board was developed, integrating tuning, matching, decoupling, RF filtering, and preamplification. Bench tests evaluated Q-factor ratio, SNR degradation under bending, phantom-based SNR, and thermal dissipation. Clinical evaluation involved hand imaging of 10 healthy volunteers (22.9 ± 0.3 years) using Cor-T1 and Ax-T2FS sequences in two positions (superman and supine). Image quality was rated by two radiologists across five tissue types using a 5-point Likert scale. Patient comfort and anxiety were assessed via post-scan questionnaires. RESULTS: In vitro tests showed a 1.6-fold SNR improvement for superficial regions (≤10 mm depth) and approximately 40% SNR loss under extreme bending, confirming robust decoupling and conformability. Radiologists reported significantly better image quality for Ax-T2FS with the flexible array, while Cor-T1 showed no significant difference. Patient comfort was markedly higher with the flexible array (85% vs. 45%), suggesting ergonomic advantages that may reduce motion artifacts. CONCLUSION: The proposed flexible 1.5T coil array enhances superficial SNR and patient comfort without compromising diagnostic quality. SIGNIFICANCE: High-density arrays of small coils can deliver clinical benefits at 1.5T, supporting their use for improved imaging in anatomically challenging regions.

items.title: How Do Users Organize Prompting Workflows in Human–AI Collaboration? A Process Mining Analysis of AI Literacy-Based Strategy Patterns
items.abstract: Growing use of large language models (LLMs) in creative and knowledge work has increased interest in how users collaborate with AI beyond output quality. This study examines how AI literacy and task type relate to prompting strategy organization, workflow, and perceptions of collaboration in ChatGPT-supported writing. Forty university students completed a divergent brand-naming and a convergent writing task. Prompting logs were analyzed using sequential pattern metrics and process mining, complemented by interviews. Higher AI literacy was associated with more structured coordination among prompting strategies, whereas lower literacy showed more repetitive, generation-centered pathways. These differences appeared in specific transition and loop configurations rather than overall transition diversity. Participants described AI as assistive, yet behavioral traces showed substantial AI contribution to outputs. These findings provide process-oriented insights into how AI literacy and task type relate to strategic adaptability in human–AI collaboration.

items.abstract: The implementation of occupational health and safety (OHS) must be examined in conjunction with labor productivity, using clear metrics. Evaluating such changes is essential to ensure that any design adjustments continue to meet technical requirements while providing a justifiable cost assessment. This study analyzes the relationship between OHS implementation and perceived productivity, and ranks OHS indicators for construction projects in Mojokerto and Jombang. A quantitative survey was conducted with 78 respondents from 20 companies, selected via purposive sampling. The research instrument included 12 OHS-related items and 13 productivity-related items, measured on a five-point Likert scale. Data analysis employed descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, Cronbach’s alpha, assumption testing, and simple linear regression. The mean scores were 4.43 for OHS and 4.35 for productivity. The resulting model is Y = 12.702 + 0.829X, with R = 0.884, R² = 0.781, and t = 16.478 (p < 0.001). Among the individual indicators, "OHS banners" ranked first, with an R² of 0.429. A significant deviation from linearity limits the interpretation of the model. The findings indicate a positive relationship within the sample, warranting further investigation using objective productivity metrics. These results suggest that the redesign process is necessary not only to adapt channel dimensions to existing site conditions but also to ensure alignment between design drawings, as-built conditions, work quantities, and cost estimates. Consequently, the evaluation of redesigns can serve as a critical component in managing scope changes for drainage projects—particularly in locations where conflicts with existing facilities or structures arise. Furthermore, these evaluations can provide a basis for verification before design changes and cost estimates are finalized for implementation.

items.title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
items.abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: S. J. Goh’s research is supported by a Startup [Grant R-314-000-110-133] and a 2021 Humanities and Social Sciences Faculty Research Fellowship from the National University of Singapore. items.title: ID-V2V: Identity-Preserving Video Restylization
items.abstract: In visual storytelling, human performances are central to creative intent and narrative meaning. However, preserving human identity and performance while enabling flexible visual edits remains challenging for generative video models. We formalize this challenge as identity-preserving video restylization, which propagates scene, lighting, and style changes specified by an edited keyframe across a source video, while preserving facial likeness and performance, including expressions, eye gaze, and lip synchronization. A key obstacle is the absence of paired training data, as identity-preserving restylized video pairs are rare in real-world settings. To address this, we propose a decoupling of source-grounded identity preservation and edit-driven video synthesis. Our key insight is that facial appearance and expression should remain invariant, with illumination being the primary permissible variation. We therefore cast identity preservation as a video relighting problem, while modeling visual edit propagation as controlled video synthesis guided by the edited keyframe. Building on this formulation, we introduce ID-V2V, a video-to-video generative framework integrating complementary control signals: relit facial regions and facial normal maps tightly constrain facial likeness and performance, while edited keyframes and depth sequences enable flexible and temporally coherent generation. This design enables constructing training pairs from a single video, eliminating the need for scarce paired data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ID-V2V significantly outperforms existing methods in preserving facial likeness and fine-grained facial performance, supports both single- and multi-subject scenarios, and delivers high visual quality, highlighting its potential as a human-centric tool for real-world content production. The code is available at: https://github.com/Eyeline-Labs/ID-V2V.

items.title: Illocutionary Explanation Planning for Source-Faithful Explanations in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
items.abstract: Natural language explanations produced by large language models (LLMs) are often persuasive, but not necessarily scrutable: users cannot easily verify whether the claims in an explanation are supported by evidence. In XAI, this motivates a focus on faithfulness and traceability, i.e., the extent to which an explanation’s claims can be grounded in, and traced back to, an explicit source. We study these desiderata in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for programming education, where textbooks provide authoritative evidence. We benchmark six LLMs on 90 Stack Overflow questions grounded in three programming textbooks and quantify source faithfulness via source adherence metrics. We find that non Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have median source adherence of 0%, while baseline RAG systems still exhibit low median adherence (22–40%, depending on the model). Motivated by Achinstein’s illocutionary theory of explanation, we introduce illocutionary macro-planning as a descriptive design principle for source-faithful explanations and instantiate it with chain-of-illocution prompting (CoI), which expands a query into implicit explanatory questions that drive retrieval. Across models, CoI yields statistically significant gains (up to 63%) in source adherence, although absolute adherence remains moderate and the gains are weak or non-significant for some models. A user study with 165 retained participants (220 recruited) indicates that these gains do not harm satisfaction, relevance, or perceived correctness. items.title: Immersive Technologies in Cockpit Interfaces of Aviation Systems
items.abstract: The article examines the transformation of flight activities in the context of developing sixth-generation human-machine systems and integrating artificial intelligence into the control of aviation equipment. The main focus is on the concept of immersive interfaces, which enable the synergistic interaction of a pilot’s cognitive, sensorimotor, and intellectual resources with the aircraft functions. Immersion of an interface is defined as an integral property characterizing the degree of a pilot’s engagement in the control space. Technological solutions for its implementation are analyzed, ranging from augmented and virtual reality systems to multimodal feedback. Particular attention is given to the analysis of professional and training immersive environments: the professional environment is aimed at improving the efficiency and safety of operator activities in combat conditions, while the training environment is aimed at developing and consolidating flight skills using simulators based on AR/VR technologies. Examples of modern aviation interfaces are considered, including the F-35 HMDS, Striker II, TARGO, TopSight, and Boeing 787 HUD, along with their ergonomic features. The article discusses the problems associated with using immersive systems, including sensory channel overload, perceptual distortion, and the risk of disorientation, as well as the technological and psychophysiological requirements imposed on them. Adaptive integration of augmented reality technologies is proposed as an optimal solution, providing a balance between efficiency, safety, and the pilot’s cognitive load.

items.title: Impact of automation conditions on task performance in the smart shopfloor digital twin interface: a function of cognitive abilities across different tasks types
items.abstract: This study aimed to investigate whether operators' cognitive abilities moderate the effects of automation level and reliability on task performance in two human-machine collaborative tasks within a smart factory's digital twin interface. Operators' cognitive abilities, including information search, spatial recognition, sustained attention, allocative attention, working memory, and spatial memory, were measured. The task performance for localisation and decision-making tasks was evaluated under varying automation levels and reliability. The results revealed distinct patterns of human-machine collaboration across the two tasks. In the localisation task, both automation level and reliability significantly influenced performance, with information search and spatial memory playing key roles. In the decision-making task, automation level had a significant impact, and spatial memorywas the only significant cognitive predictor. This study provides empirical evidence for digital twin system design and human-machine collaboration guidance based on operators' cognitive characteristics.

items.title: Impact of using the axe in motor-manual felling on hand-arm vibrations
items.abstract: Although the axe is the feller's main tool alongside the chainsaw, it has been neglected in previous studies from the point of view of occupational health and safety. The aim of the study was therefore to determine the share of axe use in the productive time of motor-manual felling and the contribution of the axe to the overall exposure of the feller to hand-arm vibration (HAV). The study was conducted during the felling of 43 spruce and fir trees with a diameter at breast height (DBH) of 11 to 90 cm using a Stihl 361 C BQ chainsaw and a conventional felling axe. The results showed that the proportion of productive time spent in axe-based operations (wedging and debarking the stump) was between 5 and 13% for spruce trees and between 2 and 7% for fir trees. The measured weighted HAV value (RMS VTV) for wedging was 6.99 m/s2 and 5.49 m/s2 for debarking the stump, which was 1.2 to 1.7 times higher than during chain-saw based operations. The contribution of the axe in the total HAV load was between 13% and 23% for spruce trees and between 6% and 18% for fir trees. The research results show that axe use contributes significantly to a feller's overall exposure to HAV, which means that the axe should be replaced by other tools or methods when felling, and research should be extended to different types of felling axes and alternatives.

items.title: Incentive Structure Shapes Mitigation Behavior in a Dynamic Landslide Risk Simulator
items.abstract: Decisions regarding mitigation and adaptation in terms of money in areas prone to landslides need to be made repeatedly. But, there is no evidence of how incentive structures of disaster insurance affect the mitigation process in dynamic environments of hazard. In the present study, mitigation and insurance decisions were studied using the Interactive Landslide Simulator, a microworld of Human Factors involving repeated decision-making under landslide risk. Seventy-five participants hailing from landslide-prone areas of Himachal Pradesh, India, were randomly allocated into No Insurance, Benevolent Insurance, or Smart Insurance groups and asked to perform 36 rounds of decision-making. It was found that insurance structure affected both mitigation and insurance investments. While the highest level of mitigation was observed in case of no insurance, Smart Insurance resulted in maximum insurance investment but did not enhance mitigation over Benevolent Insurance. Findings suggest that reimbursement-system design can shape risk-management behavior in disaster-risk policy.

items.title: InstantMimic: A High Performance System for Learning Physics-based Skills in Seconds
items.abstract: Physics-based character control is a long-standing challenge in computer graphics and robotics, requiring policies that satisfy complex dynamics while producing realistic motion. Recent Deep RL approaches, particularly imitation learning methods such as DeepMimic, have had broad impact beyond animation, influencing robotics by enabling agile and expressive behaviors. While these approaches achieve impressive results, they remain computationally inefficient to train in practice. Despite GPU-accelerated simulation, we find that end-to-end pipelines often underutilize hardware due to overheads outside the physics solver, caused by fragmented GPU kernels and CPU memory access in the critical path. We present InstantMimic, a system that addresses these inefficiencies by making the entire training loop GPU-native. Built on a GPU-native physics backend, our unified pipeline integrates simulation, environment computation, policy inference, and policy updates within a single execution flow. As a result, InstantMimic reduces training time for diverse physics-based skills to a few seconds and makes LLM-agent-driven hyperparameter search practical.

items.title: Investing in human capital: a scoping review of health programs and interventions to enhance managers’ well-being
items.abstract: Human capital is a core determinant of organizational performance, positioning managers’ health as a strategic priority for sustainable development. This scoping review aims to map and synthesize existing health programs and interventions designed to promote managers’ well-being, thereby providing an evidence-informed foundation for the development of effective health promotion strategies. This scoping review was conducted in 2025 in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A systematic search was performed across PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science using predefined keywords related to managerial health and workplace interventions. Of the 4,202 records identified, 29 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the final analysis. The included studies revealed a wide range of interventions targeting managers’ health across multiple levels. Organizational-level strategies focused on modifying the internal work environment through ergonomic interventions, such as standing desks, and cultural initiatives, including the promotion of active working practices and tobacco-free policies. Beyond the workplace, external support mechanisms such as partnerships with sports clubs and financial subsidies for physical activity were commonly reported. At the individual level, interventions encompassed educational programs, life skills training, personalized counseling, and motivational sessions aimed at stress management and lifestyle improvement. In addition, several studies incorporated diagnostic and clinical components, including the use of accelerometers, clinical screenings, and periodic health assessments to objectively monitor health risks. Promoting managers’ health requires an integrated, ecosystem-oriented approach that simultaneously addresses four interconnected domains: the internal organizational environment, the external environment, individual-level interventions, and clinical monitoring. Investment in such comprehensive health programs extends beyond ethical responsibility, representing a strategic organizational priority that can enhance productivity, support innovation, and reduce long-term operational costs. items.title: Is vibe coding the future? An empirical assessment of LLM generated codes for construction safety
items.abstract: The emergence of vibe coding, a paradigm where non-technical users instruct Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate executable codes via natural language, presents both opportunities and risks for the construction industry. While empowering construction personnel such as the safety managers, foremen, and workers to develop tools and software, the probabilistic nature of LLMs introduces the threat of silent failures, wherein generated code compiles runs without error but executes flawed mathematical safety logic. This study empirically evaluates the reliability, software architecture, and domain-specific safety fidelity of 450 vibe-coded Python scripts generated by three frontier models, Claude 3.5 Haiku, GPT-4o-Mini, and Gemini 2.5 Flash. Utilizing a persona-driven prompt dataset (n=150) and a bifurcated evaluation pipeline comprising isolated dynamic sandboxing and an LLM-as-a-Judge, the research quantifies the limits of zero-shot vibe codes for construction safety. The findings show a statistically significant association of moderate strength between user persona and data hallucination; the generated tools invented missing safety variables more often for the less formal and less specific prompts of the field personas. Furthermore, while the models demonstrated high foundational execution viability (~85%), execution success did not indicate correct logic, and error handling was present in only 16% of scripts. Among successfully executed scripts, the study identified an ~45% overall Silent Failure Rate, with GPT-4o-Mini generating mathematically inaccurate outputs in ~56% of its functional code. The results indicate that the evaluated LLMs, used without safeguards, do not provide the deterministic reliability required for standalone safety engineering. items.title: Keeping humans in the loop: AI-assisted curriculum at program scale
items.abstract: As universities adopt generative AI for curriculum development, a central risk is that efficiency gains may come at the expense of educational judgement, disciplinary expertise and human connection. Yet the same technology, used selectively, can free academics to focus on how students think and solve problems (Truu, 2026). This poster presents a programmatic, human-led method for AI-assisted course development used across UNSW College’s new Applied Degrees: industry co-designed, work-blended bachelor programs in business and information technology. It addresses two questions: how can generative AI support curriculum development at program scale while preserving human educational judgement; and where must that judgement be structurally embedded? The method is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang, 2011) and human-centred AI (Le Dinh et al., 2025), applied at program rather than course level. The main focus is programmatic coherence. Rather than building courses one at a time, the method applies shared design patterns across an entire program. Even with different subject matter experts (SMEs) and program leads contributing to different courses, these design principles remain consistent from first year to capstone. AI generates content within this architecture, but functions as a structured design assistant rather than an autonomous author. Different workflow stages route to different AI models suited to each context. This preserves checkpoints where human framing and contextual judgement re-enter the process, consistent with calls to keep human control central to AI in education (Alfredo et al., 2024; Bearman et al., 2023; Hau, 2025; Islam, 2026). The human-led, AI-supported workflow moves from industry and academic SME input and course overview revision through curriculum blueprinting, assessment critique, rubric development, Canvas-ready asynchronous content, workshop planning, and student-facing resources. The assessment-critique stage is especially significant as generative AI reshapes what assessment must do, with recent scoping evidence showing AI is driving a re-examination of assessment design across student, teacher and institutional levels (Chiu et al., 2024). Human judgement remains decisive throughout: SMEs establish disciplinary intent; program leads review coherence and progression; learning designers evaluate scaffolding, accessibility and learner experience; and final quality assurance confirms alignment before publication. The ASCILITE Technology Enhanced Learning Accreditation Standards (TELAS, 2022) informed the design from the outset and now provide the basis for review, making quality auditable. This matters for Applied Degrees, where quality depends on integrating academic standards, industry relevance, work-integrated learning and inclusive learning design. Outputs are structured for continuous improvement in Canvas, keeping pedagogical authority close to the point of delivery rather than locked inside opaque AI outputs (UNESCO, 2023). Critically, automating the repetitive build frees human effort for the work most often skipped under time pressure: the programmatic view, gathering student feedback, time with industry to collect current case studies and simulations, and targeted employability development so graduates are work ready. AI can accelerate curriculum production while strengthening human-centred design, provided the architecture and its checkpoints are designed first. The contribution is that architecture. The design patterns, curriculum blueprinting and checkpoints where human judgement re-enters are transferable to other program-scale builds regardless of which AI tools are used.

items.title: Künstliche Intelligenz in der Produktionstechnik: Potenziale, Anwendungen und gesellschaftliche Perspektiven
items.abstract: This chapter conceptualizes artificial intelligence (AI) in production engineering as a sociotechnical innovation. AI not only promises efficiency gains but also fundamentally reorganizes knowledge, work, and responsibility. Three case studies from assembly planning, laser beam welding, and predictive maintenance illustrate how algorithmic systems interact with embodied experiential knowledge and which value-laden decisions are embedded in objectives, thresholds, and routines. The analysis links technical core intuitions with perspectives on tacit knowledge, rationalization, and situated practice. A synthesis reveals three key tensions: the transformation of experience into formalized model knowledge, the shift of responsibility towards system design and operation, and the change in competency profiles towards data literacy and judgment competence. Regulatory requirements and organizational governance provide the guardrails for legitimacy and safety. From this, design principles are derived for trustworthy, auditable, and empowering AI that consistently combines transparency, human oversight, qualification, and organizational embedding.

items.title: Large language model generation of plausible semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems
items.abstract: Parsons problems have been widely recognised to support novice learners by reducing the cognitive demands of writing code from scratch through rearrangement of provided code blocks. A common variation includes distractors – erroneous blocks of code which do not belong to the correct solution. While Parsons problems have been widely studied for introductory programming, they remain underexplored in various domains including in data science education, where students may possess statistical knowledge but limited programming experience. Developing distractors is also time-consuming for educators. This study investigated the feasibility of using a large language model (LLM) to generate semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems. A set of distractors was generated for 315 Python-based data science Parsons problems and was evaluated for pedagogical plausibility, compilability, and output divergence. Validated distractors were then incorporated as exemplars in a refined prompt to generate a second set of distractors, which were evaluated using the same criteria. The findings demonstrate that LLMs can be used to develop semantic distractors for data science Parsons problems and refining the prompts using validated exemplars further improved the quality. This study contributes to the limited literature on data science Parsons problems, distractor design and LLM-supported development of these problems.

items.title: Large Language Models and Their Architectures for Machine Translation
items.abstract: Machine translation (MT) is the automatic conversion of text or speech from one language to another without human intervention. It has evolved from rule-based systems to data-driven methodologies, with neural machine translation (NMT) being a pivotal advancement in translation. Transformer is an encoder–decoder-based deep neural network, which is specifically designed for NMT. Large language models (LLMs) are based on transformer architecture and have deep bidirectional encoding and attention heads, enabling them to learn cross-lingual relationships. LLMs can perform translation through zero-shot and few-shot prompting. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is another way to use LLMs for MT systems, relying on knowledge sources like knowledge graphs and unstructured text documents that do not require specific training. Fine-tuning pretrained LLMs on a specific corpus can improve the efficacy of MT systems. LoRA (low-rank adaptation) and QLoRA algorithms can be used for fine-tuning parameters, reducing memory footprint requirements.

items.title: Large language models-as-a-judge validity is strongly task-dependent across physics assessment formats
items.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for automated assessment and feedback, understanding when LLM marking is valid is essential. We evaluate LLM-as-a-judge marking across four settings spanning three assessment formats - structured questions, written essays, and scientific plots - comparing GPT-5.2, Grok 4.1, Claude Opus 4.5, DeepSeek-V3.2, Gemini 3 Pro, and committee aggregations against human markers under blind, solution-provided, false-solution, and anchored conditions. We distinguish absolute accuracy from rank-order agreement, since a marking system can match the distribution of human marks while failing to order responses by quality. Across task types, performance is sharply task-dependent. For blind university exam questions ( n = 771 ) and secondary and university structured questions ( n = 1151 ), models show robust rank-order agreement with human markers (Spearman ρ > 0.6 ), with official solutions reducing error and strengthening agreement. False solutions degrade absolute accuracy, showing that models defer to provided references, but leave rank-ordering intact. Essay marking behaves fundamentally differently. Across n = 55 scripts, each containing five essays ( n = 275 essays total), blind AI marking is harsher and more variable than human marking and adding marking guidance does not improve rank-order agreement. Anchored exemplars shift the AI mean close to the human mean and compress variance below the human standard deviation, but rank-order agreement remains near-zero. For code-based plot elements ( n = 1400 ), models achieve high rank-order agreement ( ρ > 0.83 ) with near-linear calibration. LLM marking validity depended strongly on the assessment task, and this held for every contemporary model tested. The results also show that the reliability of the human benchmark constrains the claims that can be made about AI-human agreement.

items.title: Latent profiles of artificial intelligence ethical awareness and their association with professional identity among nursing interns: A multicentre cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Background: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into nursing education and clinical practice, nursing interns need to recognise and address ethical issues associated with its use. However, heterogeneity in their AI ethical awareness remains poorly understood. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of AI ethical awareness among nursing interns, examine factors associated with profile membership, and compare professional identity across profiles. Methods: A multicentre cross-sectional study was conducted among 550 nursing interns from 12 hospitals in China between September and October 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic characteristics, AI ethical awareness, attitudes towards AI use in nursing, ethical sensitivity, and professional identity. Latent profile analysis was performed using the mean scores of six AI ethical awareness domains. Profile characteristics were compared using chi-square tests and Welch's analysis of variance. Factors associated with profile membership were examined using R3STEP multinomial logistic regression, while differences in professional identity were assessed using the Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars method. Results: Three profiles were identified: consistently low awareness (C1; n = 152, 27.6%), autonomy–education salient (C2; n = 232, 42.2%), and consistently high awareness (C3; n = 166, 30.2%). The three-profile model demonstrated the lowest AIC, BIC, and sample-size-adjusted BIC, with an entropy of 0.876. Educational level, prior AI-related education, AI familiarity, AI tool-use frequency, attitudes towards AI use in nursing, and ethical sensitivity were associated with profile membership in at least one pairwise comparison ( p < 0.05). Attitudes towards AI use in nursing and ethical sensitivity were associated with all three pairwise comparisons. Professional identity scores were lowest in C1 (59.06 ± 7.77), intermediate in C2 (61.15 ± 8.14), and highest in C3 (63.33 ± 7.89). Significant differences were observed across profiles (Wald χ² = 23.739, p < 0.001), with all pairwise comparisons remaining significant after Holm adjustment. Conclusions: A one-size-fits-all approach to AI ethics education may not adequately address nursing interns' diverse learning needs. Nursing educators could consider tailored educational strategies that emphasise critical evaluation of AI-generated information and ethical issues related to transparency, accountability, and algorithmic fairness. Further longitudinal research is warranted to clarify the relationship between AI ethical awareness and professional identity. Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

items.title: Learning 3D Editing without Paired Supervision via Generative Prior Distillation
items.abstract: Instruction-guided 3D editing is essential for interactive content creation, yet it faces a significant bottleneck: the severe scarcity of high-quality paired training data. Existing approaches attempt to bypass this by either relying on slow test-time optimization or training on pseudo-pairs constructed via complex pipelines, which often introduce structural drift and geometric artifacts. In this paper, we propose a novel framework that learns feed-forward 3D editing without paired 3D supervision via Generative Prior Distillation. Instead of relying on ground-truth 3D pairs, our core idea is to distill visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from powerful foundation models directly into a 3D editing model. Specifically, through a differentiable rendering pipeline, we supervise the 3D representation using two complementary signals: a 2D visual prior from an image editing model at the main editing view, and a semantic prior from a Vision-Language Model at novel views to ensure strict instruction following and source identity preservation. Crucially, to address the geometric collapse and multi-view inconsistencies inherent in 2D projection supervision, we introduce a 3D-aware Distribution Matching regularization. Acting as a geometric prior, this term operates in the 3D latent space, constraining the edited output to remain within the manifold of realistic 3D assets defined by a pretrained image to 3D teacher model. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves superior instruction fidelity and cross-view consistency, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. Our project is available at: https://github.com/thiamine128/PriorEdit3D.

items.title: Learning Companion for students’ critical reasoning and academic writing
items.abstract: The advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) transformed technology’s role in the education sector by introducing highly adaptive, interactive tools. Standard implementations are often inadequately designed to effectively aid students. In some cases, these systems hinder genuine learning by inducing cognitive offloading, offering immediate solutions that bypass the cognitive processes necessary for deep conceptual understanding. This concern highlights the need for pedagogically grounded systems that foster genuine understanding and skills development. To address this gap, this paper presents an experimental implementation evaluating the feasibility of embedding formal educational frameworks directly into AI system architecture. We introduce Learning Companion, a prototype engineered to mitigate passive cognitive offloading by translating educational theory into programmatic workflows. Rather than replacing educators or automating learning, the Learning Companion is designed to strengthen meaningful learning interactions by positioning AI as a collaborative partner that supports learner agency through guided dialogue and adaptive instructional scaffolding. Aimed at enhancing critical reasoning and academic writing, the system operationalises Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) through algorithmic Socratic questioning to provide structured instructional scaffolding. This human-centred approach demonstrates how AI can complement teaching and foster deeper learner engagement while preserving meaningful connections between students, educators, and intelligent learning technologies.

items.title: Learning Stratified Policies for Inference-Time Objectives
items.abstract: Inference-time scaling improves the performance of large language models by sampling multiple responses and evaluating their collective utility. However, many existing approaches obtain these samples by repeatedly sampling from a single policy. In this work, we study if the sample budget at inference time can instead be allocated across a population of policies. We introduce stratified policies, where each of $k$ learned policies contributes one response to a $k$-sample inference-time objective. We realize this policy population using separate LoRA adapters on a shared language model backbone and optimize it for pass@$k$. We theoretically motivate the approach by analyzing the linear setting; a population of LoRAs can achieve zero best-of-$k$ approximation error in settings where every single LoRA has strictly positive prediction error. Empirically, we demonstrate that stratified policies consistently improve pass@$k$ over a single-policy baseline across multiple reasoning tasks. Overall, our results highlight how distributing samples across complementary policies can be a more effective use of sample budget than repeated i.i.d. sampling from a single policy at inference time.

items.title: Legal Awareness and Responsible Responses to AI Generated Misinformation in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence can produce convincing misleading text and synthetic media, raising questions about how people assess and respond to online information. This study examines self-reported awareness of possible legal consequences and three distinct responses to potentially false content: considering harm before forwarding, reporting deceptive material and correcting or removing content later found false. It analyses 385 adult, AI-aware questionnaire records from a Bangladesh sample comprising law students, graduates, legal professionals and other respondents. Because the questionnaire does not measure the frequency of exposure to AI misinformation or observed social media activity, the study assesses stated awareness and self-reported practices rather than exposure or actual conduct. Items are analysed separately using descriptive distributions, paired comparisons and exploratory Spearman correlations with Holm adjustment. Legal-consequence awareness was endorsed by 244 respondents (63.4%); consideration of harm by 269 (69.9%); reporting by 268 (69.6%); and correction or removal by 259 (67.3%). Awareness and reporting showed a small positive rank correlation (ρ = .138), whereas the relationships with harm consideration and correction were uncertain after adjustment for three tests. Differences between correlation coefficients require direct comparison; statistical significance in one association alone does not demonstrate a difference across practices. The findings do not show that legal awareness causes responsible behaviour. The article integrates information credibility, media literacy and the theory of planned behaviour as perspectives for a future study with measured exposure, validated items and observed verification tasks.

items.title: Legal Regulation of Autonomous Vehicles: Theoretical Bases for Systematization and International Experience
items.abstract: Objective: to study national and international approaches to regulating the operation of autonomous vehicles in order to determine the appropriate legal form of international unification and systematization of legislation in the field of autonomous transport. Methods: the methodological basis of the work was formed by a doctrinallegal approach combined with general scientific methods of cognition, including analysis and synthesis, induction and deduction, systemicstructural and formal-legal approaches. The main special method was comparative-legal one. It allowed classifying the national regulatory models of individual jurisdictions and comparing modern international legal acts developed by relevant international organizations in relation to various types of autonomous transport. Results: the study identified and characterized four regulatory approaches of states to the legalization of autonomous vehicles: the adoption of policies and strategic documents, the adaptation of current transport legislation, the introduction of experimental legal regimes, and the adoption of special laws on autonomous vehicles. It was proved that overcoming the fragmentation of legal regulation, strengthening public trust in artificial intelligence technologies and coordinating the interests of the state, business and consumers is difficult to achieve through the mechanical incorporation of disparate acts, and this requires codification. It was shown that a single codified act based on sectoral principles can ensure internal consistency of norms, unity of terminology and consolidation of the rights, duties and guarantees of subjects at the stages of design, certification, implementation and commercial operation of autonomous systems. This conclusion is confirmed by an analysis of the initiatives of the World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations of the UN Economic Commission for Europe and the International Maritime Organization. Scientific novelty: a theoretical-legal concept of systematization and codification of legislation on autonomous vehicles was developed. The concept integrates the principles of public law – transparency, accountability and protection of public interests – into the mechanism of legal regulation of intelligent transport systems. A three-level system of balancing public, private and interstate interests is substantiated. The study proposes object areas and structural parameters of a unified code covering issues of legal liability, security certification and data management. Practical significance: the formulated conclusions and proposals can serve as a methodological basis for overcoming regulatory gaps and eliminating collisions that can stifle technological innovation or pose threats to road and maritime safety. The results can be used by national legislators and international regulators in designing codified acts that provide legal certainty for manufacturers and operators of autonomous vehicles while maintaining state supervision and protecting citizens’ rights.

items.title: Legal Regulation of Content Moderation in Social Networks: Balance of Public and Private Interests under the Algorithmic Management
items.abstract: Objective: to study current technological and legal concepts in order to determine the legal nature of content moderation in social networks, choose appropriate means of its regulatory regulation, and establish the boundaries of government interference in the activities of digital platforms. Methods: the methodological basis of the work was a set of general scientific methods of cognition (analysis, synthesis, induction and deduction) in combination with special legal methods, including formallegal and comparative-legal. The use of the comparative-legal method made it possible to compare the regulatory models of Russia, China, the European Union, and the United States. The interdisciplinary approach allowed evaluating algorithmic filtering and commercial moderation from the standpoint of public-law and civilistic doctrines. Results: it is proved that moderation of user content is an element of corporate governance of a social network and an integral part of its business model. It was established that, in legal terms, this activity is implemented in three aspects: as a public-law instrument for suppressing the dissemination of illegal content in the interests of state and public safety; as a constitutional-legal guarantee of freedom of speech and fundamental rights of citizens; as a private-law mechanism for protecting the property and personal non-property rights of users and online communities. It is proved that, under hybrid information filtering with artificial intelligence algorithms, the legitimacy of platform control is achieved by a combination of legislative regulation, corporate selfregulation and, user self-censorship. Scientific novelty: the study formulates the concept of balancing the publiclaw goals of suppressing illegal information and protecting the private interests of digital content creators while limiting the discretionary powers of platform owners. The applicability of a private-law approach to content moderation relations is substantiated, including when transferring the functions of checking and blocking materials to external contractors on outsourcing terms, where a third party is actually given public-law powers without direct contractual relations with the user. The article substantiates considering artificial intelligence in the moderation circuit as an element of a sociotechnical system that affects public trust and reliability of the information environment. Practical significance: this is due to the presence of gaps in legislation regarding the regulation of platform moderation procedures, as well as the lack of regulatory certainty of the user’s right to receive an explanation of the reasons for restricting access to content and the right to challenge the decisions of algorithmic systems or moderators. The formulated conclusions can be used by the legislator and operators of digital platforms in improving the legal mechanisms of transparency, accountability and proportionality of content moderation in social networks.

items.title: Liquid biopsy in breast cancer: multi-analyte biomarkers, artificial intelligence, and precision oncology from early detection to therapeutic intervention
items.abstract: Breast cancer (BC) remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality, driven largely by tumor heterogeneity, clonal evolution, and therapeutic resistance. Tissue biopsy, while the diagnostic gold standard, offers only a static snapshot of a constantly evolving disease, and repeated sampling is often impractical, particularly in metastatic settings. Liquid biopsy has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative capable of capturing this evolving biology in real time through circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), circulating tumor cells (CTCs), and extracellular vesicles (EVs). This review examines the biological features, analytical technologies, and clinical applications of these analytes in BC, with particular attention to two rapidly evolving areas. First, we discuss how artificial intelligence and machine learning are being applied to multi-analyte liquid biopsy data, from methylation- and fragmentomics-based classifiers for early detection to models integrating ctDNA and CTC information for resistance profiling and treatment-response prediction, while critically examining current limits in clinical validation and interpretability. Second, we address the role of serial ctDNA monitoring in the neoadjuvant setting, where it can refine risk stratification beyond pathologic complete response and identify candidates for early therapeutic escalation, reflected in intervention trials now testing this approach prospectively. We also cover established roles of these analytes in treatment monitoring, minimal residual disease (MRD) detection, resistance tracking, and metastatic disease management, alongside persistent barriers to routine adoption, including limited early-stage ctDNA shedding, clonal hematopoiesis, and inconsistent analytical standardization. As these technologies mature, liquid biopsy is poised to move from a prognostic tool toward one that guides personalized treatment in BC. Not applicable. This article is a narrative review. Liquid biopsy enables longitudinal profiling of breast cancer biology. ctDNA, CTCs, and EVs provide complementary biological information. ctDNA detection can precede breast cancer relapse by approximately 10–12 months. PADA-1 showed improved PFS with plasma-guided ESR1-directed switching. Multi-analyte approaches may improve prediction beyond single biomarkers.

items.title: LMLineage: Content Lineage and Context Governance for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Interpretability for AI agents should not be confined to understanding the model's internal weights. It must also cover the agent's reasoning and decision-making process over multi-source context. We present LMLineage, an out-of-band system that attributes every output sentence of an agent session to its supporting input spans with calibrated confidences, without requiring white-box access to the model or any additional inference passes. On top of the lineage metadata, we build concept-drift micro compaction: instead of waiting for the context-length limit and summarizing everything, the system detects when previously used input documents have stopped being referenced ("drifted") and surgically compacts only those, preserving user instructions verbatim. We evaluate on a multi-tier corpus: 71 gold annotated sentences from 10 Chinese web-QA cases, plus 90 turns of independently collected multi-turn sessions across three generator models (gpt-4o-mini, qwen3.8-27b, deepseek-v4-flash). Results show that (i) window-level embedding similarity is far better aligned with LLM paraphrasing than whole document or lexical matching; (ii) the greedy-window fast path is both faster and more accurate on average than exhaustive line-matching (a multiple-comparisons bias in the latter inflates web recall at the cost of overall accuracy); (iii) per-turn attribution completes in 1s on a single GPU, remaining stable as context accumulates to 40 turns; and (iv) concept-drift detection is conservative (0% false compaction) with recall bounded by attribution accuracy. We further describe the concept-drift micro compaction design and an interactive incident-tracing/memory-cleaning case study. A companion patent application covers the lineage construction method.

items.title: Making programming learning visible: Students’ perceptions of an authentic, process-oriented assessment design
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has increased questions about whether a final code artefact alone can constitute sufficient evidence of student learning in programming education. This poster presents a practice-based evaluation of a redesigned second-year programming unit that incorporated multiple forms of evidence of learning. The assessment design is informed by authentic assessment (Boud & Molloy, 2013), feedback for learning (Carless & Boud, 2018) and self-explanation theory (Chi et al., 1989). It responded to current calls for assessment reform in the age of AI by shifting attention from the final artefact to the processes through which students design, explain, test and improve code (Lodge et al., 2023). Across three progressively sequenced assessments, students produced working Python programs, submitted WakaTime development records, recorded video explanations of design decisions, declared and justified GenAI use where permitted, and revisited prior code to improve exception handling and pytest testing. GenAI was allowed under accountable-use conditions, during which students were required to identify GenAI-assisted code, ensure that their submissions used concepts taught in the unit, and demonstrate that they understood and could explain the code they submitted. Assessment 1 established foundational object-oriented programming practices. Assessment 2 asked students to build a weather-data bot using CSV data, web scraping, datetime, logging, collections and pandas analysis. Assessment 3 required students to return to their Assessment 2 codebase and use feedback from Assessment 2 to strengthen its robustness through built-in exceptions, custom exceptions and tests. The design operationalised process-oriented assessment at task level. Code provided product evidence; WakaTime provided process evidence; video explanation provided conceptual evidence; and feedback with staged task design supported iterative development. Together, these tasks created an evidentiary architecture that made programming processes, conceptual reasoning and judgement more visible than final code alone. The evaluation drew on 68 anonymous unit feedback responses. Open-ended feedback was examined using thematic analysis (Clarke & Braun, 2017). Three student-perception themes were emergent. First, authentic tasks positioned programming as professional practice: students valued project-based tasks such as CSV analysis, web scraping and data-processing bots because they resembled meaningful programming work. Second, explanation and process evidence made computational thinking visible: students described shifts from writing code to thinking in terms of modularity, validation, debugging and engineering practice. Third, feedback supported iterative improvement and confidence: students reported that feedback helped them identify errors, revise code and progress more independently. The poster argues that process-oriented programming assessment should not rely only on restricting AI use. Instead, assessment can require multiple forms of evidence to validate student learning (Dawson et al., 2024) such as working code, development traces, self-explanatory video, feedback uptake, accountable AI-use declarations and testing artefacts. Video explanation is especially important because it prompts students to justify programing structures, methods, strategies and data-analysis approaches (Lai & Niblock, 2024). The study is limited by its reliance on one unit, one teaching period and self-reported student feedback. Further analysis of WakaTime data, video explanations, code revisions and pytest artefacts will examine how process evidence relates to conceptual understanding, reasoning and feedback uptake.
